cards.explanation: The answer is helping the wicked. Jehu, the seer, goes out to King Jehoshaphat of Judah and asks, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 19:2). It's a question, and a pointed one. Jehu says it straight to the king's face, friends, which takes some nerve.

The word is wrath. Jehu the seer tells King Jehoshaphat, “Because of this, the wrath of the LORD is upon you.” (2 Chronicles 19:2). Those are heavy words for a king to hear after he's back in Jerusalem. Hold on, friends, because Jehu isn't done talking.

The answer is True! Right after the hard word, Jehu says to the king, “However, some good is found in you…” (2 Chronicles 19:3). That “however” matters, friends. Jehu names the correction and the good in the same breath.

The good Jehu names is that Jehoshaphat removed the Asherah poles. Jehu says to the king, “…you have removed the Asherah poles from the land and have set your heart on seeking God.” (2 Chronicles 19:3). Jehu credits him with taking those poles out of the land. He says it right alongside the hard word, so both are on the table.

He turns the people back to God. The text says Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, “…turned them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.” (2 Chronicles 19:4). That's a lot of ground, friends, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim. And the text says he went out “once again,” so this wasn't the first time he went out among the people.

The answer is the LORD. Jehoshaphat tells the judges he has appointed, “…you are not judging for man, but for the LORD, who is with you when you render judgment.” (2 Chronicles 19:6). That changes how heavy every ruling feels. It also means they're never judging alone.

The reason he gives is that with the LORD there is no partiality or bribery. Jehoshaphat tells his judges, “Be careful what you do, for with the LORD our God there is no injustice or partiality or bribery.” (2 Chronicles 19:7). The judges are judging for the LORD, so their judging should look like His. Nobody gets special treatment in that courtroom.

The answer is True! In Jerusalem, King Jehoshaphat appointed “…some of the Levites, priests, and heads of the Israelite families to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes.” (2 Chronicles 19:8). So the priests are right there in the mix, friends. It's a mixed group, with Levites, priests and family heads all named.

The answer is False. Jehoshaphat tells the Jerusalem judges that every dispute counts, “…whether it regards bloodshed or some other violation of law, commandments, statutes, or ordinances…” (2 Chronicles 19:10). Bloodshed is on the list by name. It's a heavy one, friends, and the judges are told to take it seriously.

The word is guilt. King Jehoshaphat tells the Jerusalem judges to warn the people, “…so that they will not incur guilt before the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:10). He adds that wrath won't come on the judges and their brothers either. Warning the people is part of the job, friends.

The answer is Amariah the chief priest. Jehoshaphat tells the Jerusalem judges, “Note that Amariah, the chief priest, will be over you in all that pertains to the LORD…” (2 Chronicles 19:11). Matters of the LORD go to the chief priest. The king's matters go to someone else, friends.
